Description
Unite Procurement UK Limited (part of Unite Holding SE), on behalf of the Ministry of Defence, is seeking suppliers to join the Unite Procurement Platform.
The authority requires the supply of a standardised package of Army-branded clothing. Providing practical, recognisable and consistent clothing for public-facing recruitment and engagement events, routine travel and outdoor activity.
A consistent clothing package is required to improve professional presentation, support Army branding and provide practical clothing suitable for the environments in which the teams operate.
Provide a consistent and professional Army identity across Arms & Services Engagement Teams.
Provide practical clothing suitable for travel, public events and outdoor engagement activity.
Deliver a one-off issue that requires no ongoing maintenance, repair or replacement commitment from the Authority.
Included: manufacture, Army branding, packaging and delivery of complete clothing packages in the sizes confirmed by the Authority.
Included: one coordinated delivery, unless an alternative delivery schedule is agreed in writing by the Authority.
Excluded: recurring supply, replacement for loss or damage, repair, laundering, alteration after acceptance, and ongoing stock management.

The Contractor shall provide complete clothing packages. Each package shall contain:
One quilted puffer jacket.
One softshell jacket.
One pair of stretch trousers.
Three moisture-wicking T-shirts.

The Unite Procurement Platform
(Unite | Simplify indirect procurement with our smarter platform) offers a compliant route to market for UK Public Sector organisations to manage low-value, high-volume procurement.

Suppliers are encouraged to express their interest by the stated closing date to ensure early consideration. Oakengates Town Council is looking to appoint a qualified and experienced event management company to organise and deliver a carnival and parade in Oakengates, Telford in the Summer of 2027 (date to be agreed).

Avon and Wiltshire Mental Health Partnership NHS Trust (AWP) provides mental health services across Bath and North East Somerset, Bristol, North Somerset, South Gloucestershire, Swindon and Wiltshire, from more than 90 community and inpatient sites and through partnerships with external organisations. Services include acute mental health, recovery, liaison and dementia services, forensic services, Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services and a range of highly specialist mental health services.
AWP is currently in segment 3 of the NHS Oversight Framework and rated Amber-Green under the Provider Capability assessment. Following a Care Quality Commission inspection in 2024, reported in May 2025, the Trust's well-led rating was 'requires improvement'. AWP operates across two financially challenged Integrated Care Systems and works with the South West Provider Collaborative for mental health services.
The Board has invested in strengthening external stakeholder relationships and reviewing partnership working models. It has also experienced material membership changes since the previous well-led inspection, including a new Chair in autumn 2024 and three new Non-Executive Directors commencing in 2026.
AWP now requires an independent, developmental review of leadership and governance against the Care Quality Commission well-led framework. The review will provide objective and constructive challenge, identify prioritised developmental actions and inform targeted improvement work to secure and sustain future performance.

Description
The B55 and B55.2 demolition project at Sellafield involves the controlled demolition and dismantling of the B55 Office Complex and B55.2 Turbine Hall, located within the WAGR complex, down to existing ground-floor slab level. The scope includes soft stripping, asbestos remediation, high-reach mechanical demolition of the structural frame, cladding and reinforced-concrete floors, together with segregation and processing of demolition arisings, backfilling of voids and final site clearance.
A key constraint is Substation 65, which is located within the B55/B55.2 structure and must remain operational and be protected from demolition impacts, dust and water ingress throughout the works. Retained basements and associated structures also require protection, while uncertainties associated with ageing structures, buried services, below-ground voids and incomplete historical information must be managed through robust surveys, demolition engineering and risk-informed planning.
Overall, the project is intended to provide a safe, demolition-led solution that reduces workforce exposure, removes redundant infrastructure and supports accelerated hazard reduction across the wider WAGR decommissioning programme.

The Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust wishes to establish a Framework Agreement under the Health Care Services (Provider Selection Regime) Regulations 2023 and the Health Services (Provider Selection Regime)(Wales) Regulations 2025 (and as amended) (the PSR) for use by all Relevant Authorities (and any future successors to these organisations).
"Relevant authority" is defined in section 12ZB(7) of the National Health Service Act 2006 and in section 10A(9) of the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006. It means a combined authority, an integrated care board, a local authority in England, NHS England, an NHS foundation trust or an NHS trust established under section 25 of that Act, a county council or county borough council in Wales, a local health board established under section 11 of the National Health Services (Wales) Act 2006, a National Health Service trust established under section 18 of the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006, or a special health authority established under section 22 of the National health Service (Wales) Act 2006.
For the avoidance of doubt, any successor bodies of any of the above entities shall be entitled to place Orders and shall be deemed Relevant Authorities for the purposes of this Framework Agreement.
This framework agreement aims to provide a variety of solutions to allow organisations to maximise the capacity of their radiology departments and significantly reduce the cost of outsourced radiology services by realising the full potential of the scanning resources within the department. This will have two lots:
Lot 1 - Radiology Capacity Management Solutions
Lot 2 - Radiology Capacity Management Solutions with Rent to Own Equipment
This framework will run for a term of 4 years from the  commencement date of 1 September 2025. New entrants will join for the remainder of the term.

Description
County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust (CDDFT) are seeking to appoint a single supplier to provide Teleradiology Reporting Services.  The Trust operates across two large acute sites and several non-acute sites, serving the population of County Durham and Darlington.
At County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, our vision is to deliver care which is right first time, every time. We are guided by our core values of respect and dignity, compassion, quality care, improving lives, everyone counts and working together for patients.
By placing people and communities at the heart of all that we do, we strive to create a supportive and inclusive environment for both patients and our workforce, ensuring that every individual receives safe, compassionate and joined-up care.
Reporting requirements will include but are not limited to: MRI, CT, Plain Film, Nuclear Medicine, with limited reporting requiring Specialist Radiologists.
The Trust are seeking a supplier who is able to provide reporting services twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week for Urgent and Emergency Radiology Reporting, as well as provide Elective Reporting. There is no volume commitment as part of this contract and the demand from the Trust may vary overtime dependent on in house reporting capacity. However, the supplier would hold an exclusive contract for the out of hours provision to maintain continuity on the basis that the supplier can meet the turnaround time outlined by the Trust. However, for all other reporting, the Trust will be able to use alternative suppliers if desired. As demand fluctuates, the supplier must be able to adapt to high and low demands for reporting services.
Bidding suppliers will be evaluated in line with the below Provider Selection Regime (PSR) Key Criteria regulated scoring:
1:   Quality and Innovation: 20%
2:   Improving Access, Reducing Health Inequalities and Facilitating Choice: 15%
3:   Integration, Collaboration and Service Sustainability: 15%
4:   Value - Price: 40%
5:   Social Value: 10%

The provision of security services for the British High Commission (BHC) Singapore is critical to the FCDO's operational capability.
The BHC Singapore requires a reliable, professional and resilient security guarding service to protect its people, premises, operations and assets. The service will operate within a diplomatic environment and must be capable of responding to a varied and evolving threat context while maintaining appropriate standards of discretion, customer service and operational readiness. The requirement is expected to include routine guarding and access-control duties, effective incident response, support for official events and visits, and the ability to provide additional personnel at short notice.

Engagement process description
The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) will hold an initial online-only information event for its Security Guarding Services for BHC Singapore procurement on 05 November 2026, from 16:00-17:00 Singapore time (08:00 GMT).
Suppliers are invited to express their interest in attending by completing and submitting the Preliminary Market Engagement Questionnaire at:
https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/EW1ruNkgFH
by 12 noon UK time on Wednesday 04 November 2026.
Please note: You cannot attend the online event if you are not registered.
Following the information event, the FCDO will host interested suppliers at the BHC in Singapore for a 1:1 meeting w/c 16/11/2026. The format of the 1:1 will be shared with suppliers who book a 1:1 slot. You do not need to have attended the information event in order to attend a 1:1 with the FCDO.
Suppliers are also reminded:
• If you are not already registered on the Central Digital Platform (CDP), you must do so to obtain a unique supplier identifier number, which is required to bid for FCDO contracts under the Procurement Act 2023.
• The FCDO Jaggaer portal will be used to submit your actual bid, and it will require the ID obtained from the CDP.
• Registration on Jaggaer is free and takes approximately 5 minutes.
We strongly encourage suppliers to register on both platforms (CDP and Jaggaer) early to avoid delays or disappointment when procurement documents become available.

Lawsuit Prompts Minnesota to Review Data Center Project

Lawsuit Prompts Minnesota to Review Data Center Project
A settlement in a lawsuit by a nonprofit has led the state Pollution Control Agency to oversee the environmental review of a Google data center proposed for rural Pine Island.
October 29, 2026 •
Jp Lawrence, Star Tribune
A vehicle passes along Main Street in Pine Island in February. (Carlos Gonzalez / The Minnesota Star Tribune)
Carlos Gonzalez/TNS
(TNS) — For the first time in Minnesota, a state agency will oversee the environmental review of a data center, as part of a settlement agreement announced Wednesday.
Work on a data center project
proposed by Google in rural Pine Island
cannot start until the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency completes a lengthy environmental review.
The settlement
is the result of lawsuits
brought against Pine Island and contractor Ryan Companies US by the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA).
In the lawsuit, MCEA argued city officials in Pine Island have been too hasty, using a streamlined process to approve the data center project. Construction was to begin in July.
The backstory: Wednesday’s settlement marks another chapter in the controversial saga of the proposed Google data center project in Pine Island, one of
several projects proposed and debated in communities
across the state and country.
Located about 18 miles north of Rochester, Pine Island is home to about 3,500 residents.
A data center is a room or building that contains the computers and servers that store and transmit the information used by phones and computers. Some data centers are a few servers in a room, and others are massive digital warehouses companies use for cloud computing and artificial intelligence, which demand an outsized use of resources like water and energy.
Since early 2024, developer Ryan Cos. has been working on “Project Skyway,” a 482-acre technology campus that includes data centers north of Pine Island.
Google revealed it was behind the Pine Island project earlier this year, aiming to build an 88-acre site with a 250,000-square-foot data center. Pine Island and developers say the project would include environmental protections, including more green space than required by city ordinances. City officials said the data center wouldn’t affect local utility bills and would bring tens of millions of dollars in revenue to the area. Developers have promised investments bolstering Minnesota’s clean energy grid through Xcel Energy, which would provide the center with electricity.
Our reporting shows: Some residents in Pine Island said they weren’t given enough warning that a large-scale industrial data center was coming to their small rural community. They also didn’t like that Pine Island joined other
cities across the state in signing a non-disclosure agreement
to conceal information about the project, at least initially. Google also originally disclosed few specifics about its data center, such as how much energy it needs to operate.
Data centers are sparking debate across the country. Opponents most often cite concerns around noise, pollution and energy use. Supporters say data centers could provide an economic boon to struggling communities.
Across the state, protests prompted
Google to offer concessions
ahead of
a key vote in Hermantown
, as well as a county board rejecting a project proposed by
Geronimo Power in Worthington
In Pine Island, the mayor resigned, and the city council
adopted new public comment rules for its meetings
after police were called during one debate.
Last October, MCEA filed a lawsuit against Pine Island, arguing city officials didn’t properly gauge how the large-scale data center would affect the area. Pine Island used a streamlined process to measure the data center project’s potential environmental impact.
In May, the MCEA won a temporary restraining order that halted work on the project. In addition to Pine Island, the St. Paul-based environmental advocacy group has been involved in five lawsuits involving data centers, including ones in
Hermantown
and
Monticello
What comes next: According to a copy of the settlement viewed by the Star Tribune, the MCEA agreed to drop its lawsuits and Google and Ryan Cos. agreed to go through the state’s Environmental Assessment Worksheet process.
Such reviews can take anywhere from two months to more than two years, according to
a 2011 report by the Office of the Legislative Auditor
The Environmental Assessment Worksheet will require Google and Ryan Cos. to provide more extensive information on how the project affects at least 16 different environmental and community concerns, including water and energy use and potential noise and light pollution.
The MPCA would review Ryan Cos. and Google’s plan to mitigate these concerns, and then Pine Island would have to accept their plan, before construction can begin.
The environmental review will also require a longer 60-day comment period, open to the public across the state. The settlement does not revoke previous agreements made between the city of Pine Island and the project’s developers.
The conversation: In statements, Ryan Cos. Google and Pine Island officials said they welcome additional review of their project.
“Ryan Companies is pleased that the lawsuit has been settled,” Peter Fitzgerald, senior vice president of real estate development, said in a statement.
“Google is pleased to reach a constructive resolution that allows Project Skyway to move forward in Pine Island,” said Luke Hellier, public affairs manager at Google. “The goal has always been to build world-class infrastructure while serving as a responsible neighbor and resource steward. This agreement ensures the project meets robust environmental standards while delivering local economic benefits.”
Pine Island Mayor Brandi Veith Staloch called the settlement “an important step forward.” She added: “We believe this will help ensure Project Skyway moves forward responsibly.”
Kathryn Hoffman, CEO of MCEA, said she’s proud the lawsuit led to a state agency for the first time taking over the environmental review of a data center project. Activists last year unsuccessfully pushed for a law that would have mandated state-level review for large data centers.
“We feel it’s really important that the state get involved because there are statewide implications for things like water and our energy grid and our electricity bills,” Hoffman said.
Aubree Derksen, a Pine Island resident, said she believes the settlement means Ryan Cos. and Google will “start over” and provide answers to local concerns.
“We essentially got what we asked for in the settlement agreement, which is good, because we can get some protections in place that we didn’t have before,” said Derksen, a member of “Stop the Pine Island Data Center” group.
“In a perfect world for us, Google would just go away,” she added.

GIS, Digital Tools Can Help Cities Manage Utility Systems

GIS, Digital Tools Can Help Cities Manage Utility Systems
Digital GIS solutions are being used by numerous cities to administer utility infrastructure across multiple departments, helping them to become more interconnected via improved data and operations.
October 30, 2026 •
Skip Descant
Shutterstock
By Skip Descant.
It’s not just big cities turning to digital technologies to assist in managing critical infrastructure like water lines or utility poles. Smaller municipalities are also using technology to more easily integrate systems and share data and work more efficiently.
In Chambersburg, Pa., GIS experts with the borough’s public utility are using GIS technology from Esri to manage hundreds of assets like water mains, valves, electric utility poles and more. In August, technology officials launched the
Esri ArcGIS Enterprise
, an on-premises data management system. The change moved data that was previously hosted on the Esri ArcGIS cloud platform to the borough’s own servers, said Justin Evans, GIS program manager for the borough of Chambersburg, as the municipality of 23,400 residents is officially known.
“It gives you more capability to do a lot more things with it,” Evans said.
Chambersburg is unique in that it’s the only municipality in Pennsylvania that owns and manages its own electric, water, natural gas, trash collection, sanitary sewer, storm sewer and parking.
To effectively manage these, it uses GIS technology to both map the features and hold data related to each asset. For example, when electric utility staffers go out into the field, they can click on a utility pole on a map and pull up a number of data points related to this infrastructure, such as age, height and other details like what sort of transformer is on the pole. Utility officials plan to expand those capabilities to features such as the remote operation of switches and apply the same technologies to other utility divisions.
“And we want to do that for gas and water, and maybe for storm sewer and sanitary sewer,” Evans said. “But definitely those three. We want to build a utility network around them that [has] them interact together.”
“The goal is eventually to move into these other utilities and provide them the same capabilities,” he said in a follow-up email. “For issues like water line breaks to be mitigated through the use of the software.”
This vision of a utility network that’s interconnected, digital and organized around data is generally seen as the future of public-sector utilities, as organizations of all sizes trade paper maps for tablets and work more efficiently as they turn to new and innovative uses of data to plan maintenance and operations.
“Small cities prove every day that impact is not measured by size,” said Marcella Cavallaro, director for sales growth and support at Esri, in an email. “Smaller cities have long relied on ingenuity, strong relationships, and a deep understanding of the people they serve.”
GIS helps bolster those strengths, Cavallaro said, by enabling communities to replace siloed data systems with cloud-based GIS platforms like Esri ArcGIS. This can give entire city departments access to geographic data and infrastructure assets, enabling the tech workforce and engineers along with field crews to operate better and more efficiently.
In Orangeburg, S.C., near Columbia, the state’s capital, Yamira Valles-Nevarez, business systems supervisor at the Department of Public Utilities, began actively using GIS technologies about nine years ago, when she began working with the city. Valles-Nevarez formerly served as the GIS director and CIO for the Puerto Rico Planning Board.
“One of the first tools I created was a web map with all of our data. So everyone can have equal access to the data and see the data,” Valles-Nevarez said.
At the time, data was only available to those employees based in the agency’s office and was not visible to the dozens of workers out in the field. The digital maps Valles-Nevarez helped to create are now used by everyone from customer service workers answering questions from residents, to workers out in the field searching for utility poles, water main connectors and other assets. The agency then acquired mobile devices like tablets and phones to aid their fieldwork.
Orangeburg, a city of about 14,000 residents, manages electric, gas, water and sewer utilities. Valles-Nevarez created a digital inspection management plan to ensure the city complied with federal reporting requirements.
“All of the data is digital now, so it’s very easy for them to just take the data and send it to the feds,” Valles-Nevarez said.
“The electric division used to fill out a lot of paper,” she said. “Every time the guys in the field went to do a new construction ... they have this paper that they have to fill out.”
These processes have now migrated to more online digital workflows involving data collection and the completion of required forms. In the past, it could sometimes take a week for the paperwork to make its way across the needed city offices. The modern, digital work processes have resulted in data being filed more quickly and more accurately.
“And then they have to come from the field to come to the office to bring all that paper,” said Valles-Nevarez. “So we’ve made it very easy for them to collect the data.”
GIS technology, said Evans, is used to “plan out certain projects,” in part by identifying surrounding utilities, which need to be fully understood before any digging or other activities can start.
“They use this to mark the different service lines,” Evans said. “It really helps the manpower in the field. The supervisors for all the different departments are using that to reference what’s out in the field, and how to plan for the future.”
GIS, he said, can be thought of as a system for storing and managing historical data related to systems.
“That’s how you keep data on everything,” he said, noting that without GIS the borough would not have an accurate, foundational data system to say where assets are located or to convey other data points about the infrastructure.

Iowa, Feds Collaborate on Child Welfare Information System
The state is modernizing a legacy mainframe, working with federal counterparts and participating in the Child Welfare Technology Incubator initiative from the Administration for Children and Families.
March 19, 2026 •
Skip Descant
Federal and state agencies are teaming up to develop improved child welfare management systems, in a move to spur innovation and improve operations for care providers.
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (IDHHS) has partnered with the
Administration for Children and Families
(ACF) — a division of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) — as part of ACF’s newly launched
Child Welfare Technology Incubator
. The incubator is ACF’s effort to more closely support states as they develop technology systems to manage foster care and other operations. The systems, known as Comprehensive Child Welfare Information Systems (CCWIS), are partially funded and approved by ACF.
Iowa is currently involved in developing and implementing its new CCWIS, known as VISION.
“We share ACF’s expectation that IT solutions can be built more quickly, more cost effective, and designed with the needs of the social workers at the center of the work,” Danielle Sample, IDHHS director of communications for external relations, said via email. “Based on our novel approach to designing the system prior to bringing on an IT vendor, ACF has collaborated with Iowa to expedite the approvals needed to authorize VISION.”
The VISION platform “will give workers a clearer, more streamlined view of each case by organizing all individuals, services and activities in one place and reducing time spent on paperwork,” Sample said, adding guided workflows will improve and support case management.
“The platform will also securely connect with key partner systems across areas such as education, courts, health and other services, helping workers access important information more easily and coordinate support for children and families,” she said.
Developing an effective child welfare information system is often not a technical challenge — there is no shortage of vendors anxious to land a state technology contract — but one involving process and planning, ACF officials said.
Too often, said Cody Inman, delegated commissioner for the Administration on Children, Youth, and Families, states struggle in the planning of a large, multiyear technology project that can involve multiple agencies and numerous data sources.
“States typically will put out an RFP, and say, we want to do W, Y and Z. But they’re so focused on getting the actual technology system procured that they ignore the readiness, and the actual system preparation,” Inman said. “We want to change it.”
ACF would like to collaborate with states early and often to make planning more manageable so they can implement efficiently down the road.
“We don’t see the technology as the issue. There’s plenty of tech companies out there that can solve this problem,” Inman said. “What we see as the problem is the planning, the readiness, the implementation factors leading up to that.”
The incubator process is seen as a way to work more closely and collaboratively with states, nudging them toward best practices — particularly in areas like data management — and understanding federal regulations, Inman said.
Officials in Washington, D.C., point to the Nov. 13 presidential executive order (EO)
Fostering the Future for American Children and Families
, which promotes modernization of states’ child welfare information systems, as part of the basis behind the incubator initiative.
The EO outlined a “whole government approach” to improving child welfare, not only at HHS and ACF through the modernization of child welfare systems, but across other programs in the departments of Education, Labor, Treasury, Housing and Urban Development, and elsewhere, per ACF.
The Iowa project stood out, in part, because of the thoughtful planning the state had undertaken.
“So we wanted to highlight them as a way to say, this is really good planning,” Inman said. “And they did in two years what states sometimes take four or five years with their planning. So it was more like the process they used, not the technology they used. We’re not as focused on the technology.”
The Child Protective Services team currently uses the Family and Children’s System, a mainframe in service since the 1980s, Sample said. The state has entered into a contract with Google “to develop a modern, intuitive, and fully compliant” CCWIS, she said, “built with direct input from the social workers who do the work of keeping children safe.”
VISION will transform how child welfare work is completed and enhance outcomes for children and families, officials said.
“It will give workers more time with families and provide the right information they need to do their jobs effectively,” Sample said. “Iowa’s partnership with Google will serve as a road map for child welfare IT development nationally.”

Minnesota Bill Would Modernize ‘Ridiculous’ Outdated Systems
Policy
Minnesota Bill Would Modernize ‘Ridiculous’ Outdated Systems
After years of complaints from workers, lawmakers have advanced a bill to replace outdated technology without disrupting services. Having cleared the Statehouse, it awaits the governor’s signature.
May 19, 2026 •
Ashley Silver
Before the push for a bill to modernize Minnesota’s human services technology, before the new funding structure, before the long-term plans — there were the workers, dealing with a problem that had been building for years: very outdated digital resources.
During a Minnesota House of Representatives floor session May 17, one lawmaker described what county workers have been dealing with for years — systems that slow down even the most basic tasks. Rep. Paul Torkelson, R-15B, compared the technology still in use to something from the early days of computing — specifically, a 1970s video game.
“Those of you that are old enough, you might remember the game Pong, the green screen, where the little ball goes back and forth,” Torkelson said. “Well, that’s exactly the sort of technology that our counties are using today.”
He went on to describe systems that caused workers to re-enter the same information multiple times, and navigate slow, repetitive processes that added time to already complex cases. “This is ridiculous. It’s been ridiculous for quite some time,” Torkelson said bluntly during the hearing.
Their predicament, Torkelson said, was not accidental, and lawmakers played a role in it. Over the years, he said, they have repeatedly updated programs and handed them off to agencies, asking them to “incorporate this” and “incorporate that” into systems that were already outdated.
Each change required time and money, and those resources were often “gobbled up,” leaving agencies stuck maintaining old technology. The result, he said, was years of “putting Band-Aids on these old systems instead of doing the modernization that’s necessary.”
Now, there’s a bill,
SF 334
, that might begin to turn things around, said Torkelson — who was described during the House floor meeting as its author. The bill cleared the state House and Senate this week and is headed to the governor’s desk for a signature.
SF 334 doesn’t promise an immediate transformation or try to hide the complexity of what comes next. What it would do is lay out a path forward built on coordination, oversight and foundational change over time.
Beyond a mere single overhaul, the legislation would build a framework for gradual change by creating new oversight structures — an advisory council and a legislative commission — to guide decisions, prioritize projects and monitor progress. The systems it covers aren’t limited to a single agency or platform. Per the
text
, they include “any information technology system used by counties, federally recognized Indian tribes … or the commissioners … to administer a human services program.”
Despite the bill’s momentum thus far, Torkelson acknowledged the work it would begin won’t be a quick fix. One of the biggest challenges, he said, is that the system can’t simply be turned off and replaced; rather, “the old ship has to keep on sailing,” since people rely on these services every day.
Instead of starting from scratch, officials plan to layer new technology on top of the old system — what he described as an “integration layer” that puts a more modern face on outdated software. It won’t be a full fix, he said, but it should be an improvement and provide some relief to counties while larger upgrades are underway.
The bill would devise a plan for change, but would also empower “spending $90 million or so in technology modernization,” and create a new fund, providing what the legislation calls “a funding source for multiyear modernization of human services systems.”
“Money, honestly, is a big part of the cure,” Torkelson said.
The bill would direct funding toward large-scale modernization projects — those that replace, integrate or substantially enhance legacy systems. Those improvements could range from behind-the-scenes infrastructure to tools with which workers and residents will interact directly.
It would allow for system integration, automation and data-sharing improvements, and more visible changes such as digital forms, online portals and better case management tools. At the same time, it would explicitly target the kinds of outdated processes lawmakers described — reducing reliance on manual workarounds, paper-based processes and character-based screens.
But before any money from the fund is officially set aside or committed to a project, state agencies must consult with the advisory council and complete the review process. That’s what makes this bill different, lawmakers suggested. It doesn’t just fund upgrades — it creates a structure for how those upgrades are planned, funded and evaluated.

EV Charging Is Fast, but Installing Chargers May Not Be
Transportation
EV Charging Is Fast, but Installing Chargers May Not Be
Officials at a university in Southern California thought installing a few electric vehicle chargers for a new car-share program would be an easy, uncomplicated project. Installation took nearly two years.
October 09, 2026 •
Skip Descant
By Skip Descant.
It seemed to be an easy ask. At first, a plan to install seven electric vehicle (EV) chargers at a state university in Southern California appeared to be a fairly mundane campus project.
Doing it took four years.
“It was a journey from where? Hell,” is the way
Kamal Hamdan
described the ordeal during a panel discussion at the 2026 Clean Mobility Forum in Sacramento Sept. 30. Hamdan is the inaugural director of the
Center for Innovation in STEM Education
(CISE) at California State University Dominguez Hills (CSUDH) in Carson, Calif.
CISE is a regional program designed to increase the number of teachers in STEM education, and is home to the
Toyota Center for Innovation in STEM Education
, an advanced facility that includes high-tech fabrication laboratories.
You could say it all started when educators realized students were unable to make it on time to jobs and classes at the fabrication lab.
“Many of them take two or three buses to make it from home to the university,” Hamdan said, noting that during peak travel times, buses are often full and may not stop at the bus stop, making the students late for work or classes.
The university approached Toyota to establish the
Center for Resilient, Equitable and Sustainable Transportation
to explore development of a car-share program that would include a fleet of seven EVs and seven charging stations. It all seemed fairly uncomplicated, Hamdan said.
“What could be so difficult about installing seven charging stations?” he said.
That’s when things started to go sideways.
As it turned out, the university was largely maxed out on its electric capacity, he said, and “could not even install one Level 2 charging station.”
Charging the vehicles off campus didn’t seem to be an option given the logistics and cost of having students ferry the vehicles to various sites.
The project team learned of Southern California Edison’s (SCE)
Charge Ready program
, which would assist in overcoming the hurdles — including funding — of EV charging installation.
Hamdan’s team submitted an application to SCE in August 2022. It was approved, and the charging stations became operational Sept. 2, 2026.
But in between was nearly four years to work through the agreement between SCE and the myriad layers of bureaucracy around CSUDH and the
Cal State system
, a sprawling network of 22 universities across California, serving more than 450,000 students.
“We kept going, making progress. But very slow progress,” Hamdan said. “It was tough, it was rough. It was a miserable journey. But very gratifying.”
That slow, steady progress paid off. The university’s car-share program now includes a fleet of 43 EVs and hybrids, with 25 owned by Toyota and 18 owned by the campus. The project to install seven EV chargers was greatly expanded to 200 chargers, making the university, near Long Beach and Los Angeles, an EV charging hotspot.
“So now, we don’t have to worry about expanding our fleet,” Hamdan said. “We have plenty of charging stations. No other higher-ed institution has as many charging stations on their campus as much as we do.”
The headaches Hamdan and his team at CISE encountered are often all too familiar, say others working to advance equitable mobility. One common roadblock, said Ava Yaghoobirad, community transportation equity lead at the California Air Resources Board (CARB), is liability insurance.
“It’s very expensive. It takes a significant portion of their operational budget to pay for insurance,” she said during the panel.
In the projects Yaghoobirad reviewed, auto insurance alone accounted for about 29 percent of operational costs. Insurance for electric bicycle fleets used by bike-share operations tended to range from as little as 15 percent of operational costs to “as high as 60 percent.”
“The cost burdens are particularly impactful for smaller community-based organizations,” she said. “That can affect whether or not they can even launch the service.”
Yaghoobirad’s proposal to CARB’s legal team and the California Department of General Services is to base insurance requirements on fleet size, with smaller fleets having less insurance requirements, “and those larger operations, with more exposure, more risk, that could be justified to have higher insurance requirements.”
“When insurance requirements for our grants get [to] the point where it’s so hard to obtain, and it’s so expensive, that means the clean mobility projects that we want to provide for our communities will be limited,” she said.

Phoenix-Area Group Drives Creation of Multi-City Platform
Smart Cities
Phoenix-Area Group Drives Creation of Multi-City Platform
The Connective, a regional smart city consortium in the Phoenix, Ariz., metropolitan area, is working to help local governments deploy scalable technology solutions. Its events bring together private- and public-sector leaders.
August 12, 2024 •
Julia Edinger
Phoenix-area cities are joining the pilot of a regional 311-style platform after a recent technology expo helped stimulate interest in the cross-sector endeavor, which is led by the Greater Phoenix smart region consortium known as The Connective.
The group helped drive interest in the project this spring at Connected 2024, an expo that drew public- and private-sector officials to discuss creating scalable technology solutions.
The Connective
launched in 2019
to help cities develop and scale smart solutions. Since then, local governments in the region have
learned about different technologies’ potential
through its workshops,
including — but not limited to — artificial intelligence
Connected 2024, its major event this year, hosted by The Connective partner Venture Café Phoenix, drew a mix of local government leaders and technology industry experts.
The conference reversed the typical exhibition model, Ben Williams, Connective program manager, said. Where, typically, private-sector exhibitors might have displayed products and offerings, Connected 2024 put the spotlight on cities and let them share their projects with representatives of other cities.
Cities had to meet three criteria to participate as exhibitors. First, the exhibit had to be as experiential as possible. Second, it had to demonstrate a project’s impact on services or constituents. And third, the technologies or projects on display had to be something that could be replicated in other cities.
Chandler, Ariz., was an exhibiting city. Its Chief Technology Officer Kerstin Nold said via email participating brought new technology solutions to the attention of city leaders, enabling “... increased awareness and understanding of emerging technologies, while fostering collaboration and innovation in local government.”
The event featured five cities displaying 12 projects, plus sessions educating roughly 170 attendees on what The Connective does for municipalities in the region.
One major project that moved forward at Connected 2024 is creating a regional, 311-style platform for more than 20 cities and towns, to provide a single resident-facing experience in navigating services. The idea dates back several years, but a region-specific demonstration at Connected 2024 motivated most of the area’s major cities to declare their interest in participating, Jake Taylor, The Connective’s design and technology manager, said.
Here, The Connective is working with Innocode to develop a pilot, which Taylor said is proving effective and affordable. Because of the complexity and size of the undertaking, and the number of municipalities involved, a timeline has not yet been set. Taylor said most participating cities are in the discovery phase, but a couple cities have moved into the procurement phase.
The Connective is now working on expanding in the Greater Phoenix region, to ensure all communities interested in working with it can do so, Williams said. To encourage participation, the consortium is
supporting the implementation of tech solutions
to demonstrate its value.
“So, we’re working at an individual-city scale on some projects, but always with a regional view in mind,” Williams said. “What projects can expand to benefit more, or all of, the cities within the region?” The age of cities competing or solving their challenges in isolation is over, he said; it’s “collaborate or die.”
While The Connective’s success is made possible through a hyper-regional approach, its model is shared nationally. The Connective is one of six smart coalitions around the country that have
joined together
to broaden partnerships and resources for collaboration.
This fall, The Connective will take a new approach to supporting cities. Where it has traditionally held large, regional workshops to address topics like
AI
and
digital twins
, an “AI roadshow” event series is in the works to bring the consortium directly to cities, to provide more localized support. The idea is to bring a city’s different departments together to explore how they can leverage AI to support communities. Industry experts from private-sector organizations like IBM will be on hand, too — not to pitch technology solutions, but as thought leaders participating in the conversation.
“We’re going to walk away from that with ready-to-implement solutions,” Taylor said. Two area cities so far will host the traveling series in September.

Cybersecurity Is Among Beneficiaries in $186M Idaho Award

Cybersecurity Is Among Beneficiaries in $186M Idaho Award
The state will get $185.9 million from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program. The funding will support a range of endeavors including funding cybersecurity systems for rural healthcare providers.
October 29, 2026 •
Royce McCandless, Lewiston Tribune, Idaho
(TNS) — The Trump administration announced Idaho's award for the first year of the federal Rural Health Transformation Program has been fully allocated, providing just shy of $186 million in funding dedicated to improving healthcare access in rural areas of the state.
The announcement arrives after the state committed its $185.9 million award in fiscal year 2026. Had the state fallen short in allocating the amount provided, unused funds could be allocated to other states and subsequent awards could be lowered according to the terms of the program.
The award will support a range of initiatives including funding telehealth and cybersecurity systems for rural health providers. Funding will also support the build-out of programs aimed at addressing chronic disease, behavioral health, maternal and child health as well as improvements to rural healthcare facilities and equipment.
"For many Idaho families — especially in rural areas — affordable, accessible health care is a real concern," Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a release from the Center for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). "This investment recognizes those challenges and puts resources where they're needed most. It helps strengthen local health care and ensures Idahoans can get the affordable care they need, no matter where they live."
Uses for the first-year funding award include a $897,788 sub-grant to the Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and Blind for a mobile pediatric audiology clinic, a total of $5.8 million in sub-grants for Bonner General Health, a $4.8 million sub-grant for the St. Mary's Health hospital in Cottonwood and a $1.53 million sub-grant funding a mobile dental clinic expected to serve Kootenai, Bonner and Benewah counties.
A full list of awardees is available on the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare website.
The program was established through the 2025 Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which allocated $50 billion toward a newly formed Rural Healthcare Transformation Program. The program's awards are being allocated through $10 billion increments through 2030. Half of the funding pool is allocated to states equally, while the other half is distributed according to several factors including the rurality of the state's health system and financial health of a state's rural hospitals, according to CMS.
The award announcement was touted by Idaho's congressional delegation.
"From supporting workforce development programs to deploying cutting-edge technologies, these projects will tackle some of the biggest challenges facing Idaho's rural health care system," U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo said in the release. "With more funding to come in the next few years, the Rural Health Transformation Program will permanently increase access to high-quality health care across Idaho."
"The Rural Health Transformation Program is crucial to strengthening access to healthcare in rural Idaho communities," U.S. Sen. Jim Risch said in the release.
"Rural health care is a vital issue for many Idahoans," U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher said in the release. "Through the $186 million in federal funding Idaho is expected to receive, rural communities across our state will have opportunities to strengthen the physician workforce, improve emergency communications, assess health care shortages, and modernize cybersecurity. This funding is an important investment in rural Idaho, and I'm proud to support efforts to strengthen health care in our communities."
"Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts, Idaho will receive more than $185 million through the Rural Health Transformation Program," U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson said in the release. "This historic initiative is the largest investment in rural health care in American history. I've said this since President Trump signed this tax relief into law, but this was one of the most important bills I've supported in Congress. I'm thrilled to see this funding come back to rural Idaho."
The most recent meeting of the state's Rural Health Transformation Committee, comprised of several Idaho legislators, saw a vote to transfer funds away from a rural school health program. Discussion around reallocating the next year's award amount, which has yet to be announced, is expected to take place at the next committee meeting on Nov. 19.

Chicago Flooding Gets a Closer Look With New Sensor Project
A project to analyze flooding in south Chicago will eventually consist of about 50 sensors transmitting data in real time for analysts and emergency responders.
August 13, 2025 •
Skip Descant
Chicago
David Kidd/
Governing
In addition to knowing if a neighborhood is experiencing active flooding, it helps to have a bit more data. How regularly do these events occur? Is flooding expected based on the forecast?
“The sensor is just the first part,” remarked Brandon Wong, CEO for Hyfi, a maker of flood detection technology. He went on to explain how flood sensor data can offer the kinds of analysis of weather events cities need.
The issue of flooding “is growing more and more relevant within the communities we work with. Being able to have data, see what’s going on,” said Wong, is critically important. A new pilot project launched in Chicago this week to deploy about 50 sensors across the city. The first 10 have been installed in and around the
Chatham neighborhood
in south Chicago, an area of frequent flooding.
Project partners include the city of Chicago, Hyfi and Verizon, which is funding the effort. The sensors can be easily deployed in under 20 minutes, without the need for trenching or hardwiring, said officials. They provide real-time data via Verizon’s 5G communications network.
“It’s really a proof of concept to show how technology can improve the city’s ability to respond and support residents during a flood event,” said Donna Epps, chief responsible business officer for Verizon, speaking about the Chicago pilot.
The project is similar to
one deployed in New Orleans
last year, also a partnership among the city, the United Way of Southeast Louisiana, Verizon and Hyfi. In that project, 27 sensors were deployed, with the data streamed to
Streetwise
, a consumer app available to residents.
Urban flooding has been a persistent challenge for cities. However, severe weather events have become both more common and more intense, prompting planners and others to look for tools to mitigate these dangers.
“In Chicago, it [flooding] is already an ongoing challenge,” said Brendan Schreiber, deputy commissioner and chief sewers engineer for Chicago, in an email. “We are seeing more severe rain events, which have a one percent chance of occurring in any given year. Some of these events involve more than six inches of rain falling in a short period from slow-moving storms.”
It's why the city has a well-developed emergency management plan, which officials regularly review, Schreiber added.
“We are seeing increased flooding events in the city due to climate change and have been working to adapt our infrastructure to accommodate the more intense rain events we are experiencing,” he added.
The project in Chicago will run through the end of 2026, giving the city and community organizations more data to better understand flooding, and then develop mitigation strategies.
“We are excited about the data,” remarked Nedra Sims Fears, executive director of
The Greater Chatham Initiative
, a community development organization in south Chicago. “It helps inform the work we are doing.”
The Greater Chatham Initiative already works with university partners to better understand flooding, said Fears, adding, “they have a lot of different data points, and they use that information to help inform.
“This is another set of data that’s really critical for us to understand street flooding, and how that impacts the grey infrastructure, and the green infrastructure that we are examining,” she continued.
The data tells observers not only the scope and scale of flooding, but whether it’s impacting surrounding facilities like schools, hospitals, work centers and critical infrastructure, according to Wong.
“We’re combining the sensors with the analytics to help provide a comprehensive citywide picture of what flooding may be going on at a given time,” he explained. “Then that feeds into an alert engine.”
Epps, with Verizon, described the project as a, “three-pronged approach to investing in cities to empower them to prepare, respond and recover with more confidence to natural disasters.”
“This is the technology and innovation component of that broader initiative,” she added.

New Tech Platform Will Support Childcare Subsidy Program
Whatcom County, Wash., is partnering with AidKit to run and manage a new childcare subsidy to support working families. It will build on an existing program to reach more people in need.
September 30, 2026 •
Skip Descant
Yuri Arcurs peopleimages.com
By Skip Descant.
It’s hard for county officials in Washington state to imagine how they would have put in place a new program to provide childcare support without an online digital platform.
“No way! It’s laughable!” is the way Sarah Simpson responded when asked if the county could have launched Whatcom County’s new
Kids First Child Care Subsidy Program
, without the underpinning technology. Kids First will provide cash support for qualifying families to pay for childcare at licensed providers.
Simpson serves as child and family programs supervisor for Whatcom County and was instrumental in crafting the request for proposals (RFP) when the county was searching for a technology partner that could produce a digital structure able to receive applications, review eligibility documents, handle payments to childcare providers, communicate effectively with residents and have robust fraud detection protocols.
“One of the biggest tasks we had with this was creating the request for proposals — the RFP — to say, ‘what are we looking for? What are our expectations, and standards for an organization to run this?’” Simpson said.
The county, home to Bellingham, Wash., its largest city at nearly 100,000 residents, received seven or eight proposals and selected AidKit Aug. 11
as technology partner
to manage the new program, which is expected to subsidize childcare costs for at least 1,400 children in its first full year. The nearly $7.1 million contract runs through 2028.
The Whatcom County Health and Community Services Department and AidKit are in the process of designing and building the entire program, due to go live early next year, said Cassie Manning, partner success manager at AidKit. This will include all of the public-facing materials like an online application platform, FAQs and other information.
The Kids First Child Care Subsidy Program is designed to work in partnership with the state’s
Working Connections Child Care
program, which provides a subsidy to qualifying families to help pay for childcare. Working Connections is available for families earning 60 percent of the state median income or less.
“That’s very low. We know that families in Washington state are suffering or really struggling to make ends meet when they’re at 85 percent of the state median income,” Simpson said.
The county devised a program — Kids First — to help families with children up to 5 years old earning up to 75 percent of the state median income, which comes to about $104,500 annually for a family of four.
The county program also includes what are known as “bridge payments” to childcare providers to help cover costs the state’s Working Connections program does not cover. For example, the cost of providing care for babies is higher than the cost for children who are older, county officials said.
“We know the state does not pay enough to our local providers who do take families on subsidy,” Simpson said, noting childcare providers are sometimes put in the uncomfortable position of “choosing if they’re going to take those kids or not. Or they limit how many of those kids they take. And so we wanted to also incentivize providers to also take those kids.”
Health and human services departments are generally the types of government agencies AidKit works with, Manning said, “because those are generally the departments running, in this case, the childcare infrastructure program.”
The childcare program is part of the county’s strategy to aid families and help reduce household expenses, officials said.
“What we know ... is that childcare is too expensive,” Simpson said. “And that people are making the choice between working, or having a place for children to go that’s safe and reliable.”

New Medicare System Replaces Oklahoma Executive Order
The state says a new partnership with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) gives Oklahoma direct visibility into Medicare Advantage complaints while creating a permanent oversight process.
July 15, 2026 •
Ashley Silver
Shutterstock
More than 350,000 Oklahoma seniors are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, and state officials say a new partnership with the federal government will now give them a clearer path for reporting problems — as well as give state leaders greater visibility into the issues they face.
The
Oklahoma Insurance Department
(OID), working alongside the
Oklahoma Health Care Authority
(OHCA), has launched a reporting system that allows Medicare Advantage members to submit concerns directly through the state. Those complaints are reviewed by OID staff before being forwarded to the
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
(CMS), the federal agency responsible for overseeing Medicare Advantage plans.
But the reporting system is designed to do more than collect complaints. It also gives Oklahoma officials visibility into patterns that may otherwise be difficult to spot. While CMS remains responsible for responding directly to enrollees, according to the agency, “the OID monitors trends across plans, providers and agents to flag recurring problems, such as coverage denials or misleading network claims, and hold bad actors accountable.”
According to the spokesperson, the system gives the state visibility into every complaint from the time it is submitted until it is resolved, replacing what had previously been "a general, untracked inbox."
However, the reporting system is intended to strengthen oversight beyond individual complaints, according to OHCA. The spokesperson told
Government Technology
that the process also "strengthens broker accountability by helping ensure agents aren't selling plans that lack adequate provider networks."
Earlier this year, the push for more transparency into these issues was at the center of an
executive order
from Gov. Kevin Stitt. The order was issued after concerns emerged about how Medicare Advantage plans were being administered in Oklahoma and directed state agencies to take a more active role in protecting consumers and improving oversight of Medicare Advantage plans.
But that directive has since given way to a more permanent process. OHCA says Stitt withdrew the executive order because "a permanent, collaborative framework with CMS is now in place — one that gives Oklahomans the same protections the executive order was designed to provide."
For some Oklahoma officials, the new process represents a long-sought change in how states can participate in Medicare Advantage oversight. Insurance Commissioner Glen Mulready said in a recent
news release
that he has spent years advocating in Washington for states to have a larger role in Medicare Advantage oversight.
"Since I've been in office, I have traveled each year to Washington, D.C., asking for states to have more authority in Medicare Advantage because no one understands the needs of Oklahoma seniors better than Oklahoma," Mulready said.
Although Medicare Advantage remains federally regulated, he said this partnership demonstrates "what can happen when state and federal leaders work together."

The state has released a request for proposals from vendors that can provide enterprise GenAI platforms and related services, including AI literacy support. Only the vendors that own the models need apply.
October 29, 2026 •
Julia Edinger
By Julia Edinger.
The North Carolina Department of Information Technology (NCDIT) issued a request for proposals this week for
AI
platforms and related services.
This builds on the state’s progress advancing AI. North Carolina hired its first-ever AI governance and policy executive, I-Sah Hsieh, in
March 2025
. The state’s AI Council was created in
September 2025
to advise on AI strategy and it subsequently released the state’s
AI Strategic Roadmap
earlier this year.
This RFP will help the state carry out plans in the road map, which calls on government to modernize itself and improve service delivery with AI.
RFP No. 800000
is intended to solicit offers from vendors that can provide GenAI platforms, secure model application programming interface (API) access to their frontier models, and related services — including AI literacy and upskilling to support implementation.
Vendor questions are due Nov. 9 and proposals are due Nov. 30. The timeline for the selection of finalists, negotiations and the final contract award will be announced later.
The state is only soliciting offers from the vendors that own the frontier models offered through the proposed GenAI platform and model APIs, rather than from third-party vendors providing services built on top of frontier models.
The RFP defines a frontier model as “a general-purpose artificial intelligence model developed and offered by the vendor that represents one of the vendor’s most capable current model families.” It states that such a model supports advanced capabilities across multiple domains.
The state is seeking a platform that can support an array of functions, including agents, document summarization and defensive cybersecurity use cases.
“By giving agencies a simpler path to secure, trusted AI tools, we can help our employees spend more time serving the people of our state,” NCDIT Secretary and state CIO Nate Denny said in a
statement
The state requires interested vendors to describe the GovRAMP or FedRAMP status their offering holds, or alternatively, to provide a dated road map to obtain GovRAMP authorization within two years.
Some vendors may tout their products as being ready to go into production for government, even when that is not the case, Hsieh
recently told
Government Technology
He cited an example in which the state was preparing to roll out a tool only to learn that the solution could not effectively meet public records requirements.
RFP No. 800000 clearly states that inputs and outputs are state data and may constitute public records, with retention schedules governed by the N.C. Public Records Act. Interested vendors must describe how their offering meets state public records requirements.
Beyond the model itself, the RFP also asks vendors to describe the training, onboarding and adoption services included with the proposed solutions — specifically, those that will be made available at no cost to the state.
The contract term will be three years, and the state retains the option to extend the agreement.

System Lets New York State Track Harmful Algae Blooms
A new system enables the state departments of Environmental Conservation and Health to evaluate reports of harmful algae blooms. It provides an interactive map of past and current bloom locations.
June 11, 2026 •
The Press-Republican
(TNS) — The New York Harmful Algal Bloom System is now active.
As the 2026 HABs notification season starts, the system will provide the ability to send reports of HABs to the Department of Environmental Conservation electronically via a simple user- and mobile-friendly form.
DEC and the State Department of Health work closely to evaluate HAB reports. Once confirmed, reports are posted to the NYHABS page.
The system features an interactive map of current and archived bloom locations to inform New Yorkers about potential HABs.
While cyanobacteria occur naturally, certain conditions lead to accumulations that become HABs. Blooms are likely triggered by a combination of factors, including excess nutrients, lots of sunlight, low-water or low-flow conditions, calm water, and warm temperatures.
Public awareness of HABs, what they look like and their potential impacts is the first step in protecting public health. DEC provides informational resources, such as HAB warning signs, and encourages reporting to NYHABS.
To further advance efforts to reduce and mitigate the impacts of HABs, DEC recently announced the HAB Roadmap.
It provides a comprehensive and strategic guide for DEC, the public and other researchers to further address HABs by establishing six key focus areas.
These focus areas identify objectives to improve the understanding of HAB causes, reduce impacts to health and recreation, and identify specific short- and long-term steps to take.
Additionally, DEC recently released the HAB Research Grant Program to fund research in support of the objectives of the HAB Roadmap and the research focus areas of the HABs Research Guide.
The HABs Research Guide was developed to advance the study, management and mitigation of HABs in New York state and as a resource for DEC staff; other local, state or federal agencies; and research partners to fill knowledge gaps and advance efforts to reduce HABs.
Using applied research findings, DEC has improved its monitoring efforts and developed its holistic approach to HAB management based on Clean Water Planning, long-term nutrient reduction and funding to implement nutrient reduction strategies.
Since 2021, New York awarded over $424 million in grants that support reducing the frequency of HABs by targeting phosphorus and nitrogen pollution and dedicated over $6.7 million to research and development, pilot projects and advanced HABs monitoring.

ARPA Funded Helena, Mont., HR Software, CAD, Records Systems
The capital city received nearly $8.5 million from the American Rescue Plan Act and committed it all. To date, $4.5 million has been spent on internal projects including updates to at least three areas of tech.
January 10, 2025 •
Christine Compton, Independent Record
Montana's state capitol in Helena.
Shutterstock
(TNS) — Four years after the introduction of American Rescue Plan Act funds, the city of Helena spent its $8.4 million granted money on shelters, repairs and a slew of internal projects.
Congress passed ARPA, a $1.9 trillion federal economic stimulus bill, in 2021 to aid the country's recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic and recession. Money was given to cities nationwide.
The official deadline to commit the money passed Dec. 31, 2024. Cities were allowed to obligate up to $10 million in savings.
Helena committed all $8,486,620 it received to its General Fund, city spokesperson Jake Garcin said in an email, claiming it as recovered lost revenue.
But because all the money was put into savings, it was able to be spent on city and community projects.
Since then, $4.5 million has been spent on internal projects and $2.7 million was given to Helena businesses and organizations, city documents state.
Major decisions about where and how money was spent happened at various city meetings, with the commission getting the final say.
The remaining $1,118,800 is still in the General Fund, Garcin said.
For community spending, the city funded $2,781,100 in external projects, huge chunks going toward housing and homelessness.
The largest piece, $1.58 million, went to the Rocky Mountain Development Council for the Our Redeemer's Lutheran Church housing project. The project reportedly aims to build 113 housing units.
ARPA also funded a Family Promise shelter, a Good Samaritan shelter, Helena Food Share, and a downtown restroom, among other projects supporting Helena's unsheltered.
As for the $4,586,720 spent internally, the biggest project was repairing Ten Mile Water Treatment Plant, receiving $1.8 million.
Other expenses include replacing Grandstreet Theatre's roof, funding solar projects and bailing out community waterpark Last Chance Splash, which had a $200,000 budget deficit in 2023.
It also spent $750,000 on a computer aided dispatch and records management system and nearly half a million on the Helena Civic Center's HVAC system.
Another half-million went to human resources and finance software.
Lewis and Clark County met the Dec. 31 deadline. Its $13.5 million allocation went to 54 projects.

So with respect to wildfires, I mean, I guess I think it's fair to say that California gets a lot of headlines in terms of the last couple years, but how big of a threat are wildfires in Oregon at this point in time?
Keith Hormann
Quite large. Yeah. Not so much for us since we're predominantly urban. Rural electric cooperatives, they're fighting it all the time.
As a matter of fact, I believe this season is going down as the largest wildfire season on record, I believe.
Paul Ciampoli
So just switching gears here, I want to talk about distributed energy resources and specifically solar.
In researching and preparing for this interview, you noted the solar array project, the utility has been pursuing it, and the utility received a federal grant to install a solar array in which the utility will monetize the production of it and forward the proceeds to the utility's low-income energy assistance fund to help customers pay for the electric bills.
So two questions for you.
One, can you provide additional details on the project itself, including monetizing its production, and when will the solar array be installed?
Keith Hormann
Yeah, thanks for letting me talk about it. It's kind of a really interesting and fun project for us.
We did receive a congressionally funded federal HUD grant, and this grant covers the cost to install about a 200 kW solar array. We're siting on city-owned property right next to one of our substations.
But what we're doing with it is the interesting part, that we as a utility will actually monetize the generation that comes out of it at our cost and take that funding and push that into our, we already have an existing low-income energy assistance fund, but we'll be able to add additional dollars into that.
Because as you know, with all our disadvantaged customers, everybody's trying to stretch every dollar they can these days and whatever we can do to help the folks that are struggling, we certainly want to try.
And this project fit right into that to be able to pump some more money into that fund and be able to get that distributed where it's needed.
Paul Ciampoli
And does the utility have any kind of goals or state mandates as it relates to renewable energy?
Keith Hormann
We have mandates that just became effective this last year, 2025. It's called the Renewable Portfolio Standards.
So it's a little different with us since we are predominantly hydro already -- over 90% of our generation from the Bonneville Power Administration is hydro already.
But that remaining portion, 5% has to come from renewable power, yes.
Paul Ciampoli
And I was just curious, the mechanisms under which there's going to be the monetization of the production and proceeds going to the low-income energy assistance fund.
This is the first I'd heard of such a mechanism or setup.
Do you have any sense of how unique this is?
Keith Hormann
We have an existing net metering policy in place where, as our customers install solar, we'll credit them for that and then do annual true ups.
So what we're going to do is treat it the same way that we'll just credit the generation, but we'll actually just transfer the funds inside our own accounts into our low income fund.
And I don't think I answered when it was going to be done, but it's under design right now. We're getting close to 90% design.
We expect construction to start this fall yet in winter and hopefully be online by spring is our goal.
Paul Ciampoli
Getting back to the overall mechanism, could you describe how you're communicating to your customers, you know, that the fact that funds [are] going into this low-income energy assistance fund?
Keith Hormann
Yeah, we're using the normal methods. We have a city communication team that will be pushing everything out by social media.
We actually have the Oregon congressmen are planning to be here for the ribbon cutting.
So it will get some fairly good newsworthy bits about it going out here when we get a little closer.
Paul Ciampoli
On the topic of distributed energy resources, one subject that comes up a lot of times this energy storage and not necessarily as it relates to the specific solar array, but in general, have you guys looked at energy storage as a possibility?
Keith Hormann
We have to a small degree, not to any large degree. And this project, as I mentioned, is 200 kW.
Well, you know, it'll absorb by load. It'll use some of our purchases from BPA.
So if we were to look at something larger, then yeah, battery storage would definitely be of interest.
Paul Ciampoli
And so Keith, the last question I had for you, I wanted to talk about data centers, which as you know is a really hot topic these days in the energy sector.
And you noted prior to the interview that the utility is serving a new data center.
So three questions for you.
Could you provide additional details on the data center? Also, what steps did the utility take to ensure that its customers don't face rate increases to pay for the data center?
And finally, would you tell our listeners the process for the utility in terms of working with a data center developer and any lessons learned for other smaller public power utilities that may encounter data center proposals?
Keith Hormann
Yeah, it's been quite an experience for us, as you can imagine. Being a small utility, we've had quite a learning curve.
Our city is located right next to the neighboring utilities, the IOUs, high tech sector, so there's a lot of data centers nearby.
So that spillover has come to us and we've had a lot of requests. We have one very active project, which we started back in 2021. And just coincidentally, just last, about two weeks ago, we energized the phase one of the data center.
And just to provide a little context with this one project, the first phase is about a 75 megawatt peak, 50 average megawatt project. And the second phase is larger, and it's a few years down the road. It'll be around a 200 megawatt project.
But to put that in comparison, our city, we run at about 32 average megawatts and our just peak was 62.
So this has taken us into new ground that we were very inexperienced in.
So it's been, like I said, quite a learning curve.But I think what we have learned and what I would probably recommend to everyone that is in the same situation when you don't have that prior knowledge -- bring in the experts.
The one thing that we've done very well is bring in the experts from legal, financial consulting. We brought in transmission consultants to work with our BPA issues. So without their valuable input, we'd have really struggled.
So as a result of that, we've created better line extension agreements where the data center has had to completely cover the cost of two substation expansions, a couple of miles of 345 kV distribution lines to the data center sites.
We've also created energy services agreements. We have changed our rate schedules to reflect the risks associated with the single large load and the exposure we have for the rest of the city.
So we've strived really hard from the beginning to remove as much, if not at all, risk from the rest of our rate base. I think we've achieved that fairly well.
Paul Ciampoli
And it seems like things are kind of cresting now nationwide in terms of how data center developers and utilities are kind of recognizing that they need to proactively engage and communicate with communities.
So how did that go in terms of your community and customers as it relates to this data center?
Keith Hormann
Well, there was a lot of pushback [with] the common reasons.
One of the positives with this data center developer, they are not consuming the water resource that a lot of them do.
They have a different type of method, so that's been beneficial.
And the bulk of it was industrial land that was next to a residential area.
So there's been a lot of struggle with that.
As far as the electrical side, we've been communicating with everyone that we are taking as much risk mitigation measures as possible, but we are, we have an obligation to serve.
Where I can speak to the load is basically how we treat it. It could be a data center, a food processor, or if you've ever had old trapper beef jerky, that plant is located here in Forest Grove, and they're one of our largest customers.
So we're treating it the same way.
Paul Ciampoli
And, now that you have this experience of this first data center, it sounds like there's still more possibilities in terms of, the expansion of it, but would you consider serving additional data centers or you kind of kind of leave things where they're at this point?
Keith Hormann
We'll talk to anyone that comes through the door and we take that seriously. We have an obligation to serve within our service territory.
So if you're a gas station, a residential subdivision, or a data center, we're going to speak with you and go over what's needed to move ahead with your project.
Paul Ciampoli
Well, Keith, thanks so much for taking the time to speak with us today.
It's really been an illuminating conversation, and I want to thank you again for taking the time to speak with us.
Keith Hormann
Oh, absolutely, Paul. I really appreciate this opportunity.
Paul Ciampoli
Keith, you have an open invitation to return at some point in the future as a guest, so I just wanted to put that out there.
Keith Hormann
I appreciate that. If we have some big updates, I'll reach out to you.
Paul Ciampoli
Thanks for listening to this episode of Public Power Now, which is produced by Julio Guerrero, graphic and digital designer at APPA. I'm Paul Ciampoli and we'll be back with more from the world of public power next week.
